rules.title: Prohibition on sale or use of coordinated pricing algorithms to set rents or occupancy levels
rules.requirement: No one may sell, license or otherwise provide Berkeley landlords a coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy levels for Berkeley residential units, and landlords may not use one. A covered algorithm is one that uses nonpublic competitor data less than 90 days old to recommend rents, fees, occupancy rates or other lease terms in coordination with competitors.
rules.key_value: Civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation; each month and each unit is a separate violation

coverage_conditions.text: Residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley; sellers/licensors of coordinated pricing algorithms to City of Berkeley landlords and landlords using them.

rules.exemptions: Excludes (a) products publishing aggregated, anonymous rental data that do not recommend rents, fees, occupancy rates or other lease terms; (b) products used to set rent or income limits under government affordable housing guidelines; (c) information used for market research for project financing, appraisals, or research, testing or training for software development (so long as competitor data is not an input when a recommendation is calculated). Competitor Data covers only nonpublic data less than 90 days old about properties not owned or managed by the landlord. The chapter does not regulate the amount of rent.
rules.penalty: City Attorney may sue for damages, injunctive relief, restitution/return of illegal profits and civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation; aggrieved tenants may sue landlords for injunctive relief, money damages and civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation; prevailing City Attorney or tenant is awarded reasonable attorney's fees and costs. Each month a violation continues and each unit is a separate violation.
rules.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a landlord to use a coordinated pricing algorithm described in subsection A when setting rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley.
rules.conflict_note: Document records passage to print on November 18, 2025; final adoption date and effective date are not stated in the text, so in-force status is inferred from the December 2, 2025 adoption item.

rules.title: Ronald V. Dellums Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance
rules.requirement: Berkeley rental housing providers may not ask about or use criminal history or criminal background checks in advertising, applications, tenant selection, or other decisions about current or prospective tenants. This includes refusing to rent, terminating a tenancy, or charging a higher deposit or rent based on criminal history. A landlord who takes action based on criminal history must give the applicant or tenant written notice and an opportunity to respond, and must post a required notice to applicants and tenants.
rules.key_value: Ban on criminal-history inquiries and use in rental housing; fines of $1,000-$10,000 per violation

coverage_conditions.text: Rental housing providers in Berkeley, with regard to current or prospective tenants.

rules.exemptions: Lifetime sex offenders; limited exemptions for public housing/Section 8 properties; owner-occupied properties of 1-3 units where an owner of record lives in one unit as a primary residence; units under a rental agreement allowing owners to move back per BMC 13.76.130 A.9; units occupied by existing tenants seeking to sublet or add or replace roommates.
rules.penalty: Administrative fines of at least $1,000 and up to $10,000 per violation; civil damages including actual damages or three times one month's rent; punitive damages; attorneys' fees and costs; injunctive relief.
rules.quoted_span: The Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making.
rules.conflict_note: The page states only that City Council passed the ordinance on April 14, 2020. No separate effective date is given, so effective_date is left blank.

rules.title: 2026 inflation-adjusted relocation assistance for owner move-in and Ellis Act evictions
rules.requirement: Owners who evict tenants for owner move-in, or to remove a property from the rental market under the Ellis Act, must pay relocation assistance. From January 1, 2026 the standard payment is $19,413, plus an additional $6,471 for qualifying households.
rules.key_value: $19,413 standard payment; $6,471 additional for qualifying households (1.5% CPI adjustment)

coverage_conditions.text: Tenants evicted for owner move-in or so the owner can remove a property from the rental housing market (Ellis Act).

rules.interaction: The payments are indexed annually to the CPI-U for the San Francisco-Oakland-San Jose region, and the Rent Board publishes the yearly adjustment.
rules.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance; Ellis Implementation Ordinance (Rent Board approval, October 16, 2025 Special Meeting)
rules.quoted_span: The Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance requires owners to pay tenants relocation assistance in the event of an owner move-in eviction.

rules.title: Tenant screening fee cap, receipts, credit report copy and refunds (Civil Code 1950.6)
rules.requirement: Landlords may charge a capped screening fee, $68.96 for 2026, and must give the applicant a copy of any credit report, a receipt with itemized costs, and a refund of any unused portion. A landlord may not charge the fee when no unit is available and must refund applicants not selected unless it uses a first-qualified-applicant policy.
rules.key_value: $68.96 maximum screening fee (2026)

coverage_conditions.text: Landlords charging prospective tenants a screening fee.

rules.interaction: Described on the Berkeley Rent Board page as the state-law limit. Berkeley BMC 13.78.010 requires disclosure of this cap.
rules.quoted_span: Prospective tenants should expect to receive a copy of their credit report within 7 days of receipt by the landlord, a receipt for the fee paid and an itemized list of any out-of-pocket expenses and time spent by the landlord on the screening, and a refund of any unused portion of the fee.

rules.title: Notification of state law limitation on tenant screening fees
rules.requirement: An owner who charges an applicant a screening or application-processing fee must first provide a clear and conspicuous Tenant Screening Fee Rights Statement. The owner must also state the maximum fee permitted under Civil Code 1950.6(b), either in the application or in a separate disclosure before receiving the fee.
rules.key_value: Disclosure of fee rights statement and maximum fee cap before receiving fee

coverage_conditions.text: Residential rental property in Berkeley where the owner charges an applicant a screening or application fee.

rules.interaction: Supplements the state fee cap in Civil Code 1950.6 with a local disclosure requirement. Under BMC 13.78.018 it applies regardless of contrary lease terms.
rules.quoted_span: When an owner or the owner’s agent gets a request to rent residential property in Berkeley from an applicant and the owner charges a fee to purchase a consumer credit report and to validate, review, or otherwise process an application, the owner must provide, either in the rental application or in a separate disclosure before receiving the fee, a clear and conspicuous tenant screening fee rights statement and a statement of the maximum fee cap permitted under

rules.title: Prohibition of non-refundable fees associated with existing tenancies
rules.requirement: Owners may not charge existing tenants a non-refundable fee to renew a tenancy in whole or in part. This includes fees for a roommate's departure or for adding or replacing a roommate.
rules.key_value: No non-refundable renewal or roommate fees for existing tenants

coverage_conditions.text: Existing tenants of residential rental property in Berkeley.

rules.penalty: Lease provisions that violate Chapter 13.78 are unenforceable.
rules.interaction: Local rule in addition to state law. Under BMC 13.78.018, Chapter 13.78 applies regardless of contrary contractual language.
rules.quoted_span: An owner of residential rental property (or the owner’s agent) cannot charge a non-refundable fee to any existing tenant for the purpose of renewing a tenancy, in whole or in part, including any fee associated with the departure of a roommate or to request to add or replace a roommate in a pre-existing household.

rules.title: Annual General Adjustment capped at 5% (Measure BB)
rules.requirement: The yearly Annual General Adjustment for fully covered units, set by the Rent Board using a CPI-based formula, cannot exceed 5% even if the formula produces a higher figure. Landlords with banked (unused) prior AGAs may still raise rent by more than 5% to reach the rent ceiling.
rules.key_value: AGA maximum 5% per year (CPI-based formula)

coverage_conditions.text: Fully covered units, including most units in multifamily properties built before 1980; new construction units with a certificate of occupancy issued after 1980 are only partially covered (no rent ceiling).

rules.exemptions: Partially covered units (new construction after 1980, most single-family homes and condominiums) have no rent ceiling. Banked AGAs may exceed 5% to reach the rent ceiling. Units where the tenant shares kitchen or bath with the landlord are exempt only if the landlord lived on the property at the start of the tenancy.
rules.interaction: The document does not discuss interaction with state rent-cap law.
rules.citation: Berkeley Rent Ordinance as amended by Measure BB (November 2024)
rules.quoted_span: This means that, if the formula in the Rent Ordinance results in an AGA that is greater than 5%, the AGA approved by the Board for that year can be no more than 5%.
rules.conflict_note: Text says fully covered multifamily units are those 'built before 1980' while new construction is 'certificate of occupancy issued after 1980'; the exact boundary year treatment is ambiguous.

rules.title: Nonpayment eviction requires debt of at least one month's Fair Market Rent
rules.requirement: A landlord may evict for nonpayment of rent only if the tenant owes at least one month of HUD Fair Market Rent for an equivalent-size unit in the Oakland-Fremont metro area for the fiscal year the rent is demanded.
rules.key_value: Rental debt >= one month HUD FMR (Oakland-Fremont)

coverage_conditions.text: Tenants in units fully or partially covered by the Rent Ordinance.

rules.exemptions: Exempt units (e.g., shared kitchen/bath with a landlord who lived on the property at the start of the tenancy).
rules.citation: Berkeley Rent Ordinance as amended by Measure BB (November 2024)
rules.quoted_span: For a landlord to evict a tenant for nonpayment of rent, the tenant must owe an amount of rental debt equal to or greater than one month of the Fair Market Rent (FMR) value for a unit of equivalent size in the metro area Oakland-Fremont, CA HUD Metro FMR as determined by the US Department of Housing and Urban Development for the fiscal year in which the rent is demanded.

rules.title: Security deposit cap of one month's rent (AB 12)
rules.requirement: Starting July 1, 2024, landlords may generally charge no more than one month's rent as a security deposit for furnished or unfurnished units. Last month's rent counts toward the deposit; first month's rent does not.
rules.key_value: 1 month's rent (2 months for qualifying small landlords)

coverage_conditions.text: Furnished and unfurnished residential rental units statewide.

rules.exemptions: Landlords who own only two rental properties with no more than four residential units total may charge up to two months' rent if ownership is held by a natural person, family trust, or LLC whose members are all natural persons.
rules.interaction: State law summarized on the Berkeley Rent Board page. The Rent Board cannot determine whether a landlord may charge one or two months' rent.
rules.quoted_span: Starting July 1, 2024, many landlords may only charge one month's rent for unfurnished and furnished units

rules.title: Security deposit return, itemization and photo documentation
rules.requirement: Landlords must return the deposit, or any remaining portion, within 21 days after the tenant vacates, with an itemized statement and supporting documents for any deductions. Starting April 1, 2025, landlords must photograph the unit after regaining possession and before repairs or cleaning, and must give those photos to the tenant.
rules.key_value: 21 days

coverage_conditions.text: Residential tenancies under state law.

rules.quoted_span: Starting April 1, 2025, landlords must take photographs of a unit after regaining possession, but before any repairs or cleaning for which the landlord intends to make a deduction from the security deposit.
rules.conflict_note: The page gives several dates for related requirements: proof of repairs from January 1, 2025; move-out photos from April 1, 2025; and move-in photos for tenancies beginning on or after July 1, 2025.

rules.title: Security deposit interest under Berkeley Rent Ordinance
rules.requirement: For units fully or partially covered by the Berkeley Rent Ordinance, landlords must pay tenants interest on security deposits at the end of each year. If the tenant moves out before year-end, the landlord must pay a prorated amount.
rules.key_value: Annual interest payment on deposits

coverage_conditions.text: Units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance.

rules.interaction: Adds an interest requirement on top of the state security deposit rules; it does not displace them.
rules.quoted_span: For tenancies in units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance, landlords must pay tenants interest on their security deposit at the end of each year and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before the end of the year.

rules.title: 2026 Annual General Adjustment (AGA) Order – Rent Board Regulation 1148
rules.requirement: Eligible landlords may raise 2025 permanent rent ceilings by 1.0% no earlier than January 1, 2026. The AGA is set at 65% of the Bay Area CPI increase (1.5% for July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025), and landlords must meet qualifying conditions and give tenants the required notice.

coverage_conditions.text: Eligible landlords' units subject to Berkeley permanent rent ceilings; conditions for qualifying are set out in Regulation 1148.

rules.exemptions: The 2026 AGA does not apply to tenants whose tenancy began on or after January 1, 2025 and whose rents were set under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act.
rules.interaction: The notice references the state Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act: tenancies starting on or after January 1, 2025 with rents set under Costa-Hawkins are not adjusted by the 2026 AGA. The notice does not say whether this local rule displaces any statewide cap.
rules.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization Board Regulation 1148; Berkeley Municipal Code section 13.76.110A
rules.quoted_span: At its regular meeting on October 16, 2025, the Berkeley Rent Stabilization Board adopted the Annual General Adjustment (AGA) Order for Year 2026 which will allow eligible landlords to increase the 2025 permanent rent ceilings by 1.0% no earlier than January 1, 2026.

rules.title: Rent control coverage under Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance
rules.requirement: Rent control fully applies to most units in multifamily properties built before 1980, single-family homes with tenancies that began before 1996, and rooming houses. New construction, post-1995 single-family tenancies, most condominiums, and certain subsidized units are registered but not rent controlled.
rules.key_value: Rent control applies to multifamily units built before 1980; not to new construction with Certificate of Occupancy after June 1980

coverage_conditions.text: Fully covered: most units in multifamily properties built before 1980; single family homes with current tenancies that began before 1996; rooming houses (single-family homes with five or more rooms rented individually with separate leases). Partially covered (no rent control): new construction with a Certificate of Occupancy after June 1980; single-family homes with tenancies beginning on or after January 1, 1996; most condominiums; Section 202/811 units; certain HUD-mortgage project-based subsidy units.

rules.exemptions: Golden Duplex (owner-occupied on December 31, 1979 and currently owner-occupied); units where owner shares kitchen or bath with tenant and lived there when tenancy started; tenancies started after Nov 7, 2018 on properties with an ADU where either unit is owner-occupied; university rental units such as dormitories; nonprofit cooperatives.

rules.quoted_span: Most units in multifamily properties built before 1980** Fully Covered Yes Yes Yes Yes

rules.requirement: Just cause eviction protections apply to fully and partially covered units, including new construction, post-1995 single-family tenancies, condominiums and specified subsidized units. Exempt units (e.g., Golden Duplexes, shared kitchen/bath with owner, certain owner-occupied ADU properties, dormitories, nonprofit cooperatives) are not covered.
rules.key_value: Just cause applies to both fully and partially covered units, including new construction

coverage_conditions.text: Fully covered and partially covered units, including multifamily units built before 1980, single-family homes, rooming houses, new construction with a Certificate of Occupancy after June 1980, most condominiums, and units with listed government subsidies.

rules.exemptions: Golden Duplex (owner-occupied on December 31, 1979 and currently owner-occupied); units where owner shares kitchen or bath with tenant and lived there when tenancy started; tenancies started after Nov 7, 2018 on properties with an ADU where either unit is owner-occupied; university rental units such as dormitories; nonprofit cooperatives.
rules.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance (coverage guide)
rules.quoted_span: Single family homes with current tenancies that began before 1996** Fully Covered Yes Yes Yes Yes

rules.title: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy
rules.requirement: Covered housing providers may not use a blanket ban on applicants with arrests or convictions and must review applicants case by case. When deciding eligibility or eviction, they may not consider arrests without conviction, convictions with judicial relief (such as expungement or sealing), juvenile records, or convictions more than 5 years old.
rules.key_value: No blanket criminal-history bans; convictions older than 5 years excluded

coverage_conditions.text: Housing providers receiving DND funding and/or land, or that have income restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy. The policy also applies to the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program.

rules.exemptions: The limits do not apply where there is a direct relationship between a conviction and the housing sought, or an unreasonable risk of substantial harm to the safety of others. They also do not apply to current criminal behavior.
rules.interaction: Where federal or state law imposes a conflicting criminal history requirement, the federal or state law preempts this policy.
rules.citation: Boston Department of Neighborhood Development, Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy (February 2017)
rules.quoted_span: Housing providers receiving Department of Neighborhood Development (DND) funding and/or land, or that have income restricted units created under the Boston Planning and Development Agency (BPDA) Inclusionary Development Policy will not impose a blanket policy that denies housing to anyone with arrests and or convictions.
rules.conflict_note: The document is dated February 2017 but does not state an effective date. It also has separate credit-score and credit-history rules, which fall outside the six categories and are not captured as a separate record.

rules.title: Prohibition on rental-assistance (source-of-income) discrimination in Boston housing
rules.requirement: Landlords in Boston may not discriminate against applicants or tenants because they receive rental assistance, such as Section 8, social security disability, or veterans vouchers. Refusing to accept rental assistance counts as housing discrimination.
rules.key_value: Rental assistance (e.g., Section 8 vouchers) is a protected class; refusing vouchers is discrimination

coverage_conditions.text: In the City of Boston, it’s illegal to discriminate when renting, buying, selling, or securing financing for any housing.

rules.interaction: The Boston Fair Housing Commission enforces local, state, and federal fair housing laws for discrimination occurring in Boston. Complaints about discrimination outside Boston go to the state.
rules.quoted_span: The landlord tells you they don't accept rental assistance. This includes Section 8 vouchers, social security disability vouchers, and veterans vouchers.

rules.title: Housing Stability Notification Act – Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources
rules.requirement: Any landlord planning to end a tenancy must give the tenant a Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources at the same time as the notice to quit or notice of non-renewal. The landlord must also submit tenant contact information and a copy of the notice to the City through an online portal.
rules.key_value: Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources delivered with notice to quit/non-renewal; copy filed with City

coverage_conditions.text: The Housing Stability Notification Act requires ALL LANDLORDS planning to end a tenancy agreement to provide the tenant with a Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources. Also applies to foreclosing owners for the City submission.

rules.penalty: Enforced by Inspectional Services Department: 1st offense warning; 2nd and subsequent offenses $300 per day. Failure to submit the information to the City may result in a fine up to $300 per day. A violation does not halt the eviction process.
rules.interaction: The rule is a notice requirement only. The page states that a landlord's violation does not halt the eviction process.
rules.citation: Boston City Ordinances Sec. 10-11.7 (Housing Stability Notification Act)
rules.quoted_span: The Housing Stability Notification Act requires any landlord to provide renters with a Notice of Tenant’s Rights and Resources when planning to end a tenancy agreement.

rules.title: Housing Stability Notification Act – Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources
rules.requirement: A landlord or foreclosing owner ending a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy, including by eviction or lease non-renewal, must give the tenant a Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources at the same time as the Notice to Quit. The landlord must also send a copy of the Notice to Quit or Notice of Non-renewal, with a Certificate of Compliance/Service, to the City's Office of Housing Stability.
rules.key_value: Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources must accompany the Notice to Quit or non-renewal notice

coverage_conditions.text: The Ordinance applies to all landlords/foreclosing owners intending to end a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy of a unit in the City of Boston.

rules.exemptions: Residences in any hospital, skilled nursing facility or health facility; and residences in a non-profit facility whose primary purpose is providing short-term treatment, assistance or therapy for alcohol, drug, or other substance abuse. The requirements may not be waived.
rules.penalty: First offense: warning; second and subsequent offenses: $300 per day (enforced by Inspectional Services Department). A violation does not halt the eviction process.
rules.interaction: This is a local notice requirement layered onto the eviction process. A violation does not halt the eviction.
rules.citation: Housing Stability Notification Act, City of Boston Ordinances Sec. 10-11.7
rules.quoted_span: The Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources must be delivered at the same time as the Notice to Quit.

rules.title: FEHA source-of-income screening protections
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not refuse to rent to, or set different terms for, applicants or tenants based on how they will pay rent, including Section 8 vouchers and other rental assistance. They also may not refuse to complete subsidy-program paperwork or advertise a preference such as "No Section 8."
rules.key_value: Source of income (including Section 8 vouchers and government rental assistance) is a protected characteristic

coverage_conditions.text: Most housing accommodations in California and most housing providers, including landlords, property managers and tenant screening companies.

rules.exemptions: An owner occupying a home and renting to one additional person may exclude applicants based on protected characteristics, but may not publish discriminatory statements, notices or advertisements.
rules.penalty: Remedies include recovery of out-of-pocket losses, an injunction, access to the denied housing, emotional distress damages, civil penalties or punitive damages, and attorney's fees.
rules.citation: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA)
rules.quoted_span: California law protects tenants from discrimination based on how a tenant will be paying rent (“source of income”).

rules.title: Prohibition on using or distributing a common pricing algorithm as part of a restraint of trade (Cartwright Act)
rules.requirement: No person may use or distribute a common pricing algorithm, meaning a methodology or software used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to influence a price or commercial term, as part of a contract, trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade. The law is not limited to rental housing.
rules.key_value: Unlawful to use/distribute common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination, or conspiracy in restraint of trade

coverage_conditions.text: Applies to any person (as defined in Section 16702, excluding the end consumer) who uses or distributes (including selling, licensing, providing access, or subscription) a common pricing algorithm used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term.

rules.exemptions: End consumers of a product or service are excluded from the definition of person.
rules.penalty: Violations of the Cartwright Act are punishable as a crime, per the Legislative Counsel's Digest.
rules.interaction: The section does not impair or limit other antitrust laws. New § 16756.1 lowers the pleading standard: a complaint need only plausibly allege a contract, combination, or conspiracy and need not allege facts excluding independent action.
rules.citation: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729(a) (AB 325, Stats. 2025, Ch. 338)
rules.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.
rules.conflict_note: The document gives no effective date. The bill was approved by the Governor and filed with the Secretary of State on October 6, 2025.

rules.title: Prohibition on coercing adoption of prices or terms recommended by a common pricing algorithm
rules.requirement: No person may use or distribute a common pricing algorithm while coercing another person to set or adopt a price or commercial term recommended by the algorithm for the same or similar products or services in California. Commercial terms include level of service, availability, and output.
rules.key_value: Unlawful to coerce another person to adopt algorithm-recommended price or commercial term

coverage_conditions.text: Persons using or distributing a common pricing algorithm who coerce another person to adopt its recommended price or commercial term for the same or similar products or services in California.

rules.exemptions: End consumers of a product or service are excluded from the definition of person.
rules.penalty: Violations of the Cartwright Act are punishable as a crime, per the Legislative Counsel's Digest.
rules.interaction: The section does not impair or limit other antitrust laws. The relaxed pleading standard of § 16756.1 applies to Cartwright Act complaints.
rules.citation: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729(b) (AB 325, Stats. 2025, Ch. 338)
rules.quoted_span: (b) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm if the person coerces another person to set or adopt a recommended price or commercial term recommended by the common pricing algorithm for the same or similar products or services in the jurisdiction of this state.
rules.conflict_note: The document gives no effective date. The bill was approved and chaptered on October 6, 2025.

rules.title: Tenant Protection Act just cause for termination of tenancy (Civil Code 1946.2)
rules.requirement: Once a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months, the owner may terminate the tenancy only for a listed at-fault or no-fault just cause, which must be stated in the written notice. For no-fault terminations, the owner must pay relocation assistance or waive the final month's rent, equal to one month's rent; curable violations require a notice to cure first.
rules.key_value: Just cause required after 12 months of occupancy (or 24 months for one tenant if adult tenants are added); no-fault relocation assistance or rent waiver equal to one month's rent, paid within 15 calendar days

coverage_conditions.text: Residential real property, including dwellings or units in a mobilehome park, after the tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied it for 12 months. If additional adult tenants are added before an existing tenant has occupied it for 24 months, coverage applies only if all tenants have 12+ months or one or more tenants have 24+ months.

rules.exemptions: Transient/tourist hotel occupancy; nonprofit hospital, religious, extended care, licensed elderly residential care, or adult residential facilities; school or higher-education dormitories; units where the tenant shares a bathroom or kitchen with an owner who resides there; single-family owner-occupied residences renting no more than two units or bedrooms (including ADU/JADU), and mobilehomes; owner-occupied duplexes where neither unit is an ADU/JADU; housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (rolling, except mobilehomes); separately alienable units not owned by a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome park management, if the required exemption notice is given; deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing; mobilehome homeowners.
rules.penalty: Noncompliance voids the termination notice. An owner who attempts to recover possession in material violation is liable for actual damages, discretionary reasonable attorney's fees and costs, and up to three times actual damages plus punitive damages for willful, oppressive, fraudulent, or malicious conduct. The Attorney General, city attorney, or county counsel may seek injunctive relief.
rules.interaction: The section does not apply to property covered by a local just cause ordinance adopted on or before September 1, 2019, or by a later-adopted or amended ordinance that is more protective (with a binding local finding); in those cases the local ordinance applies. A property cannot be subject to both. Local ordinances adopted after September 1, 2019 that are less protective are unenforceable unless this section is repealed. No-fault relocation assistance is credited against relocation assistance required by other law.
rules.citation: Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2 (as amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 203, AB 1529)
rules.quoted_span: Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.
rules.conflict_note: Subdivision (m) says the section became operative April 1, 2024. The history note says the latest amendment (Stats. 2025, Ch. 203, AB 1529) is effective January 1, 2026. The operative date from the text is used. The section is repealed as of January 1, 2030.

rules.title: Tenant Protection Act statewide rent cap (Civil Code 1947.12)
rules.requirement: Over any 12-month period, an owner may not raise the gross rent by more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, measured from the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months. A continuing tenant's rent may be raised in no more than two increments per 12 months, and the owner may set the initial rent freely for a new tenancy.
rules.key_value: 5% + CPI, max 10%, per 12 months; max two increases per 12 months

coverage_conditions.text: Residential real property, meaning any dwelling or unit intended for human habitation, including mobilehome park units. Housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years is exempt unless it is a mobilehome; this is a rolling cutoff, not a fixed date. The section applies to rent increases on or after March 15, 2019, and to mobilehome tenancies on or after February 18, 2021.

rules.exemptions: Exempt properties: (1) deed- or agreement-restricted affordable housing; (2) school and university dormitories; (3) housing under valid local rent control that restricts increases to less than this section; (4) housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years, unless a mobilehome; (5) separately alienable units such as single-family homes and condos, if the owner is not a REIT, corporation or LLC with a corporate member (or mobilehome park management) and tenants received the required written exemption notice; (6) owner-occupied two-unit structures where neither unit is an ADU or JADU; (7) mobilehome homeowners as defined in Section 798.9. Initial rent for a new tenancy is not capped.

rules.title: Security deposit capped at one month's rent

rules.penalty: Lessor forfeits the right to retain any portion of the deposit for certain violations. Treble damages of the deposit plus 5% interest, court costs and attorney's fees apply for failure to deposit properly, transfer, or return the deposit. Conflicting lease provisions are void.
rules.quoted_span: No lessor or successor in interest shall at any time subsequent to the commencement of a tenancy demand rent in advance in excess of the current month's rent or a security deposit in excess of the amount allowed by this section.

rules.title: Security deposit handling, interest and 30-day return
rules.requirement: Deposits must be held in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account, with receipts and annual interest at 5% or the bank rate. The deposit, minus only permitted deductions with a sworn itemized damage list, must be returned within 30 days after the tenancy ends.
rules.key_value: Return within 30 days; interest at 5% per year or the lesser bank rate

coverage_conditions.text: Lessors of residential real property who accept a security deposit

rules.exemptions: Vacation or recreational tenancies of 100 days or less. Successor liability does not apply to cities or towns acquiring title under chapter 60 or to certain chartered financial institution mortgagees.
rules.penalty: Treble damages plus 5% interest, court costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Forfeiture of the right to retain the deposit. The tenant is entitled to immediate return of the deposit for failure to deposit properly or to make records available.
rules.quoted_span: If the lessor or his agent fails to comply with clauses (a), (d), or (e) of subsection 6, the tenant shall be awarded damages in an amount equal to three times the amount of such security deposit or balance thereof to which the tenant is entitled plus interest at the rate of five per cent from the date when such payment became due, together with court costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

rules.title: Limit on upfront charges at start of tenancy
rules.requirement: At or before the start of a tenancy, a landlord or the landlord's agent may not require a tenant or applicant to pay more than first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit equal to one month's rent, and the cost of a lock and key. The 2025 amendment extends the limit to agents of the lessor.
rules.key_value: Upfront charges limited to first month's rent, last month's rent, security deposit (1 month), and lock/key cost

rules.title: Broker fee paid only by the party who hired the broker
rules.requirement: A rental broker's fee may be charged only to the party (landlord or tenant) who originally hired and contracted with the broker. A tenant cannot be made to pay a broker fee for a broker the landlord engaged.
rules.key_value: Broker fee payable only by the party who engaged the broker

rules.quoted_span: Any fee shall only be paid by the party, lessor or tenant who originally engaged and entered into a contract with the licensed broker or salesperson.

rules.title: Required form accompanying notice to quit for nonpayment of rent
rules.requirement: A landlord's written notice to quit a residential tenant for nonpayment of rent must include a state-developed form. The form documents any repayment agreements, gives information on rental assistance, court rules and legal limits on evictions, and states that the notice is not an eviction.
rules.key_value: Notice to quit for nonpayment must include the state form, and courts will not accept an eviction filing without proof the form was delivered.

coverage_conditions.text: Written notices to quit for nonpayment of rent given by a landlord to a residential tenant.

rules.penalty: No court with jurisdiction over summary process, including the Boston municipal court department, may accept a writ, summons or complaint for filing in a residential nonpayment eviction without proof that the required form was delivered.
rules.quoted_span: Section 31. (a) A notice to quit for nonpayment of rent given in writing by a landlord to a residential tenant pursuant to this chapter shall be accompanied by a form that shall include, but not be limited to: (i) documentation of any agreements between the tenant and landlord for the tenant to repay the landlord for nonpayment of rent; and (ii) information on: (1) rental assistance programs including, but not limited to, the residential assistance for families in transition program; (2) applicable trial court rules, standing orders or emergency administrative orders pertaining to actions for summary process; and (3) any relevant federal or state legal restrictions on residential evictions.
rules.conflict_note: This is a notice-procedure requirement for nonpayment evictions. It does not limit the permitted causes for eviction, so it fits the just_cause_eviction category only loosely.

rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act - ban on criminal-history inquiries before a conditional offer
rules.requirement: A housing provider may not ask about an applicant's criminal record, orally, in writing or on an application, until after making a conditional offer. The only exceptions are methamphetamine manufacturing on federally assisted housing premises and lifetime sex-offender registration. Before accepting any application fee, the provider must disclose in writing whether criminal history is considered and that the applicant may submit evidence of inaccuracies, rehabilitation or other mitigating factors.
rules.key_value: No criminal-record inquiry before conditional offer; written disclosure required before accepting an application fee

coverage_conditions.text: Applies to housing providers renting a "rental dwelling unit," defined as a dwelling unit offered for rent for residential purposes, other than a dwelling unit in an owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units.

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units. Providers may consider methamphetamine manufacturing or production on federally assisted housing premises and lifetime sex-offender registration.
rules.penalty: Penalties are imposed by the Division on Civil Rights; there is no private court action. They are: up to $1,000 with no prior violation within 5 years; up to $5,000 with one prior violation within 5 years; up to $10,000 with two or more prior violations within 7 years. The director may also order cease and desist, return of the application fee, a conditional offer or unit for repeat violators, and payment of up to $1,000 to the applicant.
rules.interaction: The act does not affect independent rights or actions, including those under the Law Against Discrimination, P.L.1945, c.169.
rules.quoted_span: shall not make any oral or written inquiry regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.
rules.conflict_note: The act takes effect on the first day of the seventh month following enactment, and it was approved June 18, 2021. The effective date of 2022-01-01 is computed from those two facts, not stated explicitly in the text.

rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act - limits on criminal records considered after conditional offer, and individualized assessment
rules.requirement: Providers may never consider arrests or charges without conviction, expunged, pardoned, vacated or sealed records, or juvenile adjudications. After a conditional offer, they may consider only specified serious convictions or recent indictable convictions: first degree within 6 years, second or third degree within 4 years, fourth degree within 1 year. A withdrawal of the offer requires an individualized assessment, a preponderance finding of a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest, and a written notice with an opportunity to appeal.
rules.key_value: Lookback: 6 years (1st degree), 4 years (2nd/3rd degree), 1 year (4th degree); certain serious crimes have no limit

coverage_conditions.text: Rental dwelling units, other than a dwelling unit in an owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units.

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units. With no time limit, providers may consider convictions for murder, aggravated sexual assault, kidnapping, arson, human trafficking, sexual assault, specified child sexual offenses, or any crime resulting in lifetime sex-offender registration.
rules.penalty: Penalties of up to $1,000, $5,000 or $10,000 depending on prior violations, plus remedial orders that may include return of the application fee and up to $1,000 paid to the applicant.
rules.quoted_span: A housing provider may withdraw a conditional offer based on an applicant's criminal record only if the housing provider determines, by preponderance of the evidence, that the withdrawal is necessary to fulfill a substantial, legitimate, and nondiscriminatory interest.
rules.conflict_note: The effective date is computed from 'first day of the seventh month next following the date of enactment' and approval on June 18, 2021.

rules.title: Residential rental property application fee capped at $50
rules.requirement: A landlord or its agent may not require an application or similar fee above $50 to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental unit. The cap is adjusted each January 1 by the CPI change, with adjustments made only when the CPI change is positive.
rules.key_value: $50 maximum application fee, CPI-adjusted annually

coverage_conditions.text: Residential rental property for dwelling purposes, excluding dwelling units in one-family or two-family dwellings offered for rent.

rules.exemptions: A dwelling unit in a one-family or two-family dwelling offered for rent. A New Jersey Real Estate Commission licensee, unless the licensee is the landlord of the property.
rules.penalty: Up to $500 for a first offense, up to $750 for a second offense, and up to $1,000 for each subsequent offense, enforced by summary proceedings under the Penalty Enforcement Law of 1999 on complaint of the Director of Consumer Affairs or the Attorney General. The amount wrongfully charged is taken from the collected penalty and remitted to the applicant.
rules.quoted_span: A landlord, or agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which exceeds $50.
rules.conflict_note: The text does not state a calendar effective date. The act takes effect on the first day of the fourth month following enactment, and it was approved January 20, 2026, which gives May 1, 2026. CPI adjustments begin January 1 of the year following enactment (2027).

rules.title: Security Deposit Law maximum deposit
rules.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit greater than one and one-half times one month's rent, and any yearly deposit increase may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Prepaid rent, including last month's rent, and pet deposits count toward the cap.
rules.key_value: 1.5x monthly rent; annual increase max 10% of current deposit

coverage_conditions.text: The Security Deposit Law applies to most residential rental properties, including mobile homes. The exception is an owner-occupied two-, or three-family dwelling.

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings, unless the tenant opts in by written request (applies 30 days after the request).
rules.penalty: Tenant may sue for double the amount wrongfully withheld plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1); civil penalty of $500-$2,000 per offense for willfully withholding deposits of tenants on government assistance; unlawful use of deposit monies is a disorderly persons offense (fine of not less than $200 and/or up to 30 days imprisonment).
rules.quoted_span: The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ).

rules.title: Anti-Eviction Act good cause requirement
rules.requirement: Residential landlords may not evict or refuse to renew a written or oral lease without one of the statutory good causes, and must serve a Notice to Quit (and in some cases a Notice to Cease) with cause-specific notice periods. Tenants evicted for illegal occupancy are entitled to relocation assistance equal to six times monthly rent.
rules.key_value: Statutory good causes (a)-(r); relocation assistance of 6x monthly rent for illegal-occupancy evictions

coverage_conditions.text: The Anti-Eviction Act applies to most residential rental properties including single-family homes, mobile homes and land in a mobile home park, apartment buildings, and complexes, and rooming and boarding homes.

rules.exemptions: Two- or three-unit owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units; hotel/motel guests and transient or seasonal tenants (unless the occupant has no alternate residence); units held in trust for a developmentally disabled immediate family member who permanently occupies the unit.
rules.penalty: Landlord who misuses owner-occupancy or removal-from-use grounds is liable for three times damages plus attorney fees and costs, and a civil penalty up to $10,000 per violation for residential use within five years after a removal-from-use eviction (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.6).
rules.quoted_span: No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.

rules.title: Unconscionable rent increase prohibition
rules.requirement: New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but a rent increase must not be unconscionable and must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance; a landlord may only raise rent by terminating the old lease with proper notice and offering a new lease.
rules.key_value: No statewide numeric cap; increase must not be unconscionable

coverage_conditions.text: Residential tenancies covered by the Anti-Eviction Act; municipalities may separately adopt rent control or rent leveling ordinances.

rules.penalty: Landlord cannot evict for nonpayment of an unconscionable increase; tenant may complain to a municipal rent control board where one exists.
rules.interaction: Increases must also comply with any municipal rent control ordinance where one exists.
rules.quoted_span: The increase in rent must not be unconscionable; it must not be so unreasonable as to shock the conscience of a fair and honest person and must comply with any municipal ordinances governing rent increases.

rules.title: New construction exemption from local rent control
rules.requirement: Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control ordinances for 30 years following completion of construction.
rules.key_value: 30-year exemption from local rent control after completion

coverage_conditions.text: Newly constructed multiple dwellings.

rules.exemptions: Governmentally subsidized rents may also be exempt from local rent control; HUD-owned/subsidized and NJHMFA-financed projects are not subject to municipal rent control.
rules.interaction: State law exempts these buildings from municipal rent control ordinances.
rules.quoted_span: Under the Newly Constructed Multiple Dwellings Law ( N.J.S.A. 2A:42 -84.5), newly constructed multiple dwellings shall be exempt from any local rent control ordinances for a period of 30 years following completion of construction of the building.

rules.title: No rent increases to cover conversion costs
rules.requirement: When a building is converted to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, rents may not be increased to cover costs resulting solely from the conversion, though increases for new services or amenities are allowed.
rules.key_value: No increases attributable solely to conversion costs

coverage_conditions.text: All tenants in a building being converted, regardless of protected tenancy eligibility.

rules.quoted_span: If a building is converted to a condominium or cooperative form of ownership, or to fee simple ownership of units, rents may not be increased to cover cos ts resulting solely from the conversion (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.31).

rules.title: Law Against Discrimination - source of lawful income
rules.requirement: Landlords may not discriminate in renting housing on protected bases including source of lawful income.
rules.key_value: Source of lawful income is a protected class

coverage_conditions.text: All landlord-tenant relationships, with listed exceptions.

rules.exemptions: Two-family owner-occupied dwellings, rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home, and single-sex residences (and age-restricted housing as to familial status).
rules.penalty: Monetary damages, order to rent the unit to the complainant, and fines up to $10,000 for a first offense (N.J.S.A. 10:5-14.1a(a)).
rules.quoted_span: The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD), N.J.S.A. 10:5-12(g) to -(h), prohibits discrimination when selling or renting property and requires equal treatment in the sale or rental of housing regardless of race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, mental and physical disability, nationality, or source of lawful income.

rules.title: Credit report cost and reasonable application fees
rules.requirement: Landlords may charge applicants the cost of a credit report and may request reasonable rental application fees; no specific cap is stated.
rules.key_value: Cost of credit report plus reasonable application fees

coverage_conditions.text: Prospective tenants screened via credit reports.

rules.quoted_span: The landlord is allowed to charge the tenant for the cost of the report. The landlord may also request reasonable rental application fees or employment verification.

rules.title: Source of lawful income discrimination prohibited under NJ Law Against Discrimination
rules.requirement: Landlords may not discriminate in housing based on the source of lawful income or source of lawful rent payment a tenant uses. For example, a landlord cannot refuse to rent to a Section 8 voucher holder solely because of that income source.
rules.key_value: Source of lawful income (e.g., Section 8 vouchers) is a protected basis

coverage_conditions.text: Applies to the sale or rental of all property, including open land, whether for business or residential purposes, subject to listed exceptions.

rules.exemptions: Rental of a single apartment or flat in a two-family dwelling where the owner occupies the other unit; rental of rooms by the owner or occupant of a one-family dwelling they occupy as a residence; religious organization preference for persons of the same religion; familial status protection does not apply to housing for older persons.
rules.quoted_span: This means, for example, that a landlord cannot deny the lawful recipient of a Section 8 HUD voucher the right to rent an apartment based solely on that source of lawful income.
rules.conflict_note: The document describes complaint procedures but states no specific sanction. Complaints may be filed with the Division on Civil Rights within 180 days or in Superior Court within two years.

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act – ban on algorithmic rent coordination
rules.requirement: Landlords may not pay for or use the services of a coordinator, meaning anyone running algorithmic revenue management software or an algorithmic device that performs a coordinating function. Coordinators may not facilitate anticompetitive agreements, and no person may engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination or perform a coordinating function. Violations are violations of the New Jersey Antitrust Act.
rules.key_value: Unlawful to use or perform a coordinating function via algorithmic rent-setting software or devices

coverage_conditions.text: Rental property owners of residential dwelling units (any house, apartment, accessory unit, or other unit intended as a primary residence in the State), and coordinators operating algorithmic revenue management software or algorithmic devices that perform a coordinating function.

rules.exemptions: Algorithmic device excludes non-AI spreadsheets requiring human analysis and databases that only query unprocessed data. Coordinating function excludes research, statistical analysis or testing not used to set or recommend terms; free public rent estimates; equal-terms real estate brokerage listing databases that do not set or recommend prices or collect sensitive data to do so; and government affordability controls. Government entities applying affordability controls are not coordinators. Residential dwelling units exclude inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities.
rules.penalty: Conduct is a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act (C.56:9-1 et seq.); the Act's sections 6 through 17 (C.56:9-6 through 9-17) apply to violations.
rules.interaction: State law. Municipalities may not enact ordinances that conflict with the act, except ordinances explicitly authorized or required by other law. The act adds to the New Jersey Antitrust Act and does not authorize conduct already unlawful.
rules.quoted_span: e. any person to perform a coordinating function.
rules.conflict_note: The text sets the effective date as the first day of the twelfth month following enactment, and the act was approved July 20, 2026. 2027-07-01 is calculated from that rule; the document does not state it.

rules.title: Just cause required for termination of tenancy
rules.requirement: A landlord may not terminate a tenancy without at-fault just cause (e.g., nonpayment, material lease breach, nuisance, criminal activity) or good-faith no-fault just cause (owner move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, a government order, or demolition/substantial remodel). Owner move-in for leases entered on or after June 24, 2023 requires the tenant's written agreement or an express lease provision, and the intended occupant must move in within 90 days and stay at least 12 months.
rules.key_value: Just cause required; 12 at-fault grounds and 4 no-fault grounds

coverage_conditions.text: Residential rental property (any dwelling or unit intended for human habitation, including mobilehome park units) with tenancies of more than 30 days, excluding fixed-term leases of three months or less and the exemptions in §98.0703.

rules.exemptions: Transient/tourist hotels; short-term residential occupancy; deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing (but not Section 8); Mobilehome Residency Law mobilehomes; nonprofit hospital, religious, extended care, licensed elderly or adult residential facilities and non-profit transitional housing; school dormitories; units where the tenant shares a bathroom or kitchen with a resident landlord; owner-occupied single-family residences renting no more than two bedrooms, ADUs or JADUs; owner-occupied duplexes; housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (except mobilehomes); separately alienable units not owned by a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome park management, where the tenant receives the required written exemption notice.
rules.penalty: Tenant may sue for injunctive and equitable relief and money damages, including punitive damages. Wrongful eviction damages are at least three times actual economic damages, and the court may award attorney's fees and costs. Noncompliance voids any termination notice and is an affirmative defense to eviction. The City may pursue civil and criminal enforcement.
rules.interaction: The ordinance states it requires just cause consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2 and that its rights are in addition to existing state or federal tenant rights. It does not state that it displaces the state rule. New-construction coverage uses a rolling 15-year certificate-of-occupancy exemption rather than a fixed cutoff date.
rules.citation: San Diego Municipal Code §98.0704 (O-21647 N.S.; amended O-21769 N.S.)
rules.quoted_span: A landlord shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause.

rules.title: Relocation assistance for no-fault just cause terminations
rules.requirement: For a no-fault termination, the landlord must provide relocation assistance regardless of the tenant's income or length of tenancy. At the landlord's option this is either a direct payment of two months' actual rent (three months if the tenant is a senior or disabled), paid within 15 days of the notice, or an equivalent rent waiver. Buyout agreements must exceed this amount or are void.
rules.key_value: 2 months' rent (3 months for seniors 62+ or disabled tenants)

coverage_conditions.text: Tenancies in residential rental property subject to Division 7 that are terminated for no-fault just cause.

rules.exemptions: Exemptions in §98.0703 apply. A tenant found at fault for conditions triggering a government vacate order gets no relocation assistance. Assistance is credited against other federal, state or local relocation assistance and may be recovered as damages if the tenant fails to vacate.
rules.penalty: A landlord who fails to provide required relocation assistance is liable for not less than three times the required relocation assistance plus actual economic damages, and the termination notice is void.
rules.interaction: Relocation assistance under this Division is credited against relocation assistance required by federal, state or other local law. It is in addition to the return of any deposit or security owed.
rules.quoted_span: Unless section 98.0706(c)(1)(A)(ii) applies, the direct payment to the tenant shall be in an amount equal to two months of actual rent under the tenant’s lease in effect at the date of the notice.

rules.title: Notice and re-offer requirements for no-fault terminations
rules.requirement: No-fault termination notices must be given 30 or 60 days in advance per Civil Code 1946.1, in at least 12-point font, and must state the basis, the relocation assistance, and the tenant's right to a renewal offer. If the unit is re-rented within five years after an owner move-in, government order, or demolition/remodel eviction, the landlord must first offer it to the displaced tenant, who has 30 days to accept. Landlords must also notify the Housing Commission within three business days once its portal exists.
rules.key_value: 30/60-day notice; 5-year right of first offer

coverage_conditions.text: Tenancies in residential rental property subject to Division 7 terminated for no-fault just cause.

rules.exemptions: Exemptions in §98.0703 apply. The Commission-notice requirement does not apply until 30 days after the Commission establishes a submission portal and gives public notice.
rules.penalty: Failure to strictly comply voids the termination notice. Tenant civil remedies under §98.0709 also apply, including damages, punitive damages and attorney's fees.
rules.interaction: The notice period follows California Civil Code section 1946.1.
rules.quoted_span: In addition to other remedies applicable to landlord’s failure to comply with this Division, a landlord's failure to strictly comply with section 98.0706 shall render void any notice of termination required by section 98.0706.

rules.title: Prohibition of Anti-Competitive Automated Rent Price-Fixing Ordinance
rules.requirement: Proposed ordinance making it unlawful to sell, license, or otherwise provide an algorithmic device that uses nonpublic competitor data to advise or recommend rental rates or occupancy levels to a landlord. It would also bar landlords from using such a device to set rental rates or occupancy levels for residential rental property.
rules.key_value: Ban on sale, licensing and use of algorithmic rent-setting devices; civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation

coverage_conditions.text: Algorithmic devices that use or incorporate one or more algorithms to perform calculations of nonpublic competitor data concerning rental rates, occupancy levels, or other information regarding the leasing of residential rental property, to advise a landlord on, or recommend to a landlord, rental rates or occupancy levels for residential rental property in the City of San Diego.

rules.exemptions: Software or products that publish reports on rental rates or occupancy levels from aggregated historical nonpublic competitor data more than 90 days old, or from public information, and do not recommend rates or occupancy levels for future leases or renewals. Also exempt: software used to establish rental rates or income limits under local, state, or federal affordable housing program guidelines.
rules.penalty: A tenant may sue a landlord for injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation. Each month a use violation continues, and each residential rental property involved, counts as a separate violation. A prevailing tenant recovers costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and lease clauses limiting fee recovery are unenforceable. Remedies are cumulative.
rules.interaction: Remedies are cumulative and in addition to any other remedies at law, statute, or ordinance. The ordinance does not say it displaces any state rule.
rules.citation: San Diego Municipal Code Chapter 9, Article 8, Division 11, §§98.1101-98.1104 (proposed Ordinance O-2025-107)
rules.quoted_span: It is unlawful for a landlord to use an algorithmic device to set rental rates or occupancy levels for residential rental property.
rules.conflict_note: The document is a staff report and draft ordinance with blank ordinance number and passage date. It takes effect on the thirtieth day after final passage, but no passage date is given.

rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance just cause eviction requirement
rules.requirement: A landlord may evict a tenant from a unit covered by the Rent Ordinance only for one of 17 listed just cause reasons, and that reason must be the dominant motive for the eviction. Lease expiration or a change in ownership is not just cause, and a landlord also needs just cause to remove housing services such as parking, storage or laundry.
rules.key_value: 17 just cause reasons; just cause must be the dominant motive

coverage_conditions.text: Rental units covered by the Rent Ordinance. This includes tenancies exempt from the rent increase limits, such as newly constructed units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979, tenancies eligible for rent increases under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act, and some tenancies where another government agency regulates the rent.

rules.exemptions: Under Ordinance Section 37.2(r), a landlord may temporarily remove certain housing services, such as parking and storage, to perform mandatory soft-story seismic retrofit work. The illegal-use cause does not include merely occupying an unwarranted unit or a single short-term rental violation that is cured within 30 days.
rules.penalty: A landlord who evicts or tries to evict a tenant unlawfully may be subject to substantial civil and/or criminal liability.
rules.interaction: The just cause protections extend to tenancies exempt from local rent increase limits, including Costa-Hawkins-eligible tenancies. The document does not state whether this rule displaces any state rule.
rules.quoted_span: In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction.

rules.title: Relocation payments for owner/relative move-in, demolition, capital improvement and substantial rehabilitation evictions
rules.requirement: For eviction notices served March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027 based on owner/relative move-in, demolition/permanent removal, temporary capital improvement work or substantial rehabilitation, landlords must pay $8,245 per tenant, up to $24,733 per unit, plus $5,497 for each elderly (60+) or disabled tenant or household with minor children. Temporary capital improvement evictions under 20 days are governed by state law instead, at $446/day plus actual moving expenses per household.

rules.title: Santa Ana annual maximum allowable rent increase
rules.requirement: Landlords may raise rent once each year by no more than the lesser of 3% of current rent or 80% of the CPI change. The maximum allowable increase is 2.87% for September 1, 2026 through August 31, 2027.
rules.key_value: Lesser of 3% or 80% of CPI change; 2.87% for 2026-09-01 to 2027-08-31
rules.citation: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization and Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
rules.quoted_span: The increase cannot be more than 3% of your current rent or 80% of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) change, whichever is less.

rules.title: Santa Ana just cause eviction and relocation assistance
rules.requirement: Landlords must have a valid reason to evict, such as nonpayment of rent, lease breach, or owner move-in. For certain eviction reasons, landlords may have to help pay the tenant's moving costs.
rules.key_value: Valid reason required; relocation assistance for certain evictions
rules.citation: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization and Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
rules.quoted_span: Your landlord must have a valid reason to evict you. This could be for not paying rent, breaking the lease, or if the landlord wants to move into the property themselves.

rules.title: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization Ordinance
rules.requirement: Annual residential rent increases are limited to the lower of 3% or 80% of the CPI change over the most recent 12 months, and no increase is allowed if CPI is negative. Owners may petition the City for a fair-return increase above the cap.
rules.key_value: Lower of 3% or 80% of CPI change per year; 0% if CPI negative

coverage_conditions.text: The rent cap does not apply to residential buildings constructed after February 1, 1995, or to mobile home spaces offered for rent after January 1, 1990.

rules.exemptions: Residential buildings constructed after February 1, 1995; mobile home spaces offered for rent after January 1, 1990. Owners may petition for fair-return relief, decided within 60 days of a complete application.
rules.interaction: The document does not discuss how the ordinance interacts with the statewide rent cap.

rules.title: Santa Ana Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
rules.requirement: After 30 days of tenancy, an owner may terminate only for a just cause stated in a written notice. For at-fault causes, the owner must first give a notice to cure. For no-fault causes, the owner must provide 3 months of relocation assistance or waive the final 3 months' rent.
rules.key_value: Just cause required after 30 days; 3 months relocation assistance or rent waiver for no-fault terminations

coverage_conditions.text: The Just Cause Ordinance shall not apply to certain types of residential property, including housing produced in the last 15 years; deed-restricted affordable housing; hotel and transient occupancy; hospital and care facilities; dormitories; and other shared living quarters.

rules.exemptions: Housing produced in the last 15 years (rolling); deed-restricted affordable housing; hotel and transient occupancy; hospital and care facilities; dormitories; other shared living quarters.
rules.interaction: The document does not discuss how the ordinance interacts with state just cause law.
